To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
anaerobic processes are important in the degradation of microphytotbenthic-derived organic matter in estuarine sediments.
anaerobic micro-organisms (sulphate reducers and methaogens) degrade both easily and refractory organic matter in microphytobentic biofilms.

anaerobic micro-organisms (including co-existing sulphate-reducing bacteria and methanogens), are responsible for the majority of the degradation of microphyto-benthic-derived organic carbon, with the more structurally complex, insoluble, extracellular polymeric substrates being degraded more slowly than labile, water-soluble organic matter.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the fate of organic material produced by the benthic algae that grow on mudflats.
the degradation of organic matter derived from microphytobethnic biofilms within intertidal sediment.
the fate of microphytobic biofilms in intertidal sediemnts and the role of microphytotic biofilms in carbon cycling.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
microphytobenths are an important source for organic carbon and energy for microorganisms in the intertidal sediements.
the fate of DOC and EPS fractions, which are the primary source of carbon for microorganisms, is similar under aerobic and anaerobi conditions.
microphytobentos-derived organic carbon and EPS are rapidly utilised by both oxic and anerobic microorganisms.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
anaerobic microphytobethos degradation is more complex than aerobic degradation.
anaerobic micro-organisms are responsible for the degradation of more structurally-complex components of microphytbenthic EPS.
anaerobic processes are important contributors to carbon and nutrient cycling in intertidal sedi-ments.
The main takeaway from our work is that
anaerobic processes are more important than previously thought in the fate of microphytobeathic-derived organic carbon and EPS in intertidal sedi-ments.
anaerobic microbial communities are capable of utilising more complex components of microalgal-derived EPS, and that anaerobes may be the dominant consumers of these EPS under natural conditions.
microphytobentos-derived organic matter is rapidly degraded under aerobic and anaerobe conditions and that a complex microbial community degrades both labile and recalcitrant components of EPS.
